Background (from the session that started this one):
Mahmoud said invite links must use `/m`, because `/m` is the main app and `/w` is the old classic app. PR 7935 fixed the signup survey for people who sign up on `/m`, and it left invited users on the old flow, which still sends the same PostHog survey event from `web/ee/src/components/PostSignupForm/PostSignupForm.tsx`. This invite work is separate because it changes how people join an organization and needs its own testing.

Task:
Make organization invites work on the `/m` app, so that the invite link no longer goes through the old app. Today `api/oss/src/services/organization_service.py:139` builds `<web_url>/auth?token=...&email=...&organization_id=...&workspace_id=...&project_id=...`. `isTokenBearingAuthLink` in `web/packages/agenta-shared/src/utils/mobileGate/index.ts` keeps that link on the old sign-in, and the person accepts on the old `/workspaces/accept` page (`web/oss/src/pages/workspaces/accept.tsx`). `/m` has no screen that reads the token.

Needed: the `/m` sign-in keeps the invite values through sign-in. `/m` gets an accept screen with the same behavior as the old page, including a signed-in person whose email differs from the invited email. The API builds the link with `/m/auth`, and the gate stops holding invite links on the old app, while password reset links (which also use `token`) stay where they work today. Also check what happens to an old invite link already sitting in someone's inbox.

Done means: one PR, with tests, and a live check with a new invited user and an existing user both joining through `/m`. Before building, ask Mahmoud whether new invited users should answer the onboarding questions, because they currently reach the old `/post-signup` survey form and that form would no longer run for them. Run the `build` skill; this touches access, so it is the Feature tier.

Open one PR and make it ready

Base directory for this skill: /home/mahmoud/code/agenta/.claude/skills/build

# Build router

This skill picks a workflow by the size and risk of the work, then runs it. Each workflow is a
short list of blocks, and each block is its own skill with its own gate. The workflow files are
in `workflows/` next to this file.

## Step 1: Pick the tier

Read the task, the linked issue, and the code it touches. Then go through the tiers from the
top, and take the first tier whose rules match. A task that matches any one rule of a tier goes
in that tier.

| Tier | Entry rules (any one is enough) | Workflow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Program | More than three PRs. Mahmoud wants the work split into milestones that ship separately. | `workflows/program.md` |
| Feature | One to three PRs. A new contract (API, wire field, config shape, database table). A migration. It touches access checks, credentials, billing, or the runner. It needs a product decision from Mahmoud. | `workflows/feature.md` |
| Bug | Something that should work does not, and the fix is one PR. | `workflows/bug.md` |
| Small change | One PR, under about 300 changed lines, no new contract, no migration, and it does not touch access checks, credentials, billing, or the runner. | `workflows/small.md` |

A bug whose fix needs a new contract, a migration, or a product decision is a Feature. The
"risky areas" in every workflow are access checks, credentials, billing, the runner, and
migrations.

## Step 2: Tell Mahmoud the tier in one line

Send one line, then start the workflow without waiting for an answer:

```
Tier: Feature, because it adds a field to the secrets API. Say "make it a Program" to move it up.
```

Mahmoud can move a task up a tier at any time. Move a task down only when he says so. When the
work grows past its tier while you build (a second PR, a new contract, a risky area), move it up
yourself, tell him in one line, and run the blocks the higher tier adds.

## Step 3: Run the workflow

Open the workflow file for the tier and run its blocks in the listed order. Each block names the
skill that runs it and the gate it must pass. Do not start a block whose inputs depend on a gate
that has not passed. Blocks whose inputs are ready run at the same time.

## Rules for every tier

Roles:
- The orchestrator decides and delegates. Give each subagent one narrow job with full context:
  the goal, the files and symbols, the acceptance check, and the area `AGENTS.md`. A subagent
  that must guess produces work you redo.
- Subagents report up. A subagent never starts its own fixers for side bugs it finds. It lists
  them, and the orchestrator decides.
- Models: Opus for implementation, design and verification. Sonnet for QA driving, recordings,
  labels, status edits, and other mechanical steps. The `review-loop` skill picks the review
  models.

Building:
- Read the current code before you plan. Where the code differs from the issue or an old plan,
  the code is the truth.
- Make the smallest correct change at the root cause. Match the surrounding code. Do not
  refactor next door.
- Check the property at the system boundary that ships: the wire payload, the rendered page in
  `/m` (`web/mobile`, the main app), and Daytona for anything that runs in a cloud sandbox. A
  test that only runs the changed file shows the change, not the fix. When one policy has
  several readers, check every reader.
- When the work defines or changes an interface (API params, wire field, config schema, tool
  definition, event payload), run the `design-interfaces` skill on it.
- When the change moves an interface, endpoint, config field, default, or runtime behavior, run
  the `keep-docs-in-sync` skill in the same PR.
- Before each commit: `~/.local/bin/ruff format` then `~/.local/bin/ruff check --fix` in the API,
  SDK or services folder you touched (never `uvx ruff`), and `pnpm lint-fix` in `web/` for
  frontend changes.
- A sandbox image change (`services/runner/images/sandbox/**`, `agent-requirements.txt`, harness
  pins) bumps `services/runner/config/sandbox-recipe.json` in the same PR.
- No backward compatibility shims, no runtime flag injection, and no user-facing text you made
  up. Quote every new user-facing string in your report.

Branches and PRs:
- One PR in the GitButler workspace (`~/code/agenta`): a lane made with `but branch new <name>`,
  committed with `but commit <lane> --only`. Load the `gitbutler-stacks` skill for any stacked or
  multi-lane work. Take `but oplog snapshot -m "..."` before any risky `but` operation.
- Parallel work, or a busy workspace: a separate clone or worktree, as the `milestones` skill
  describes. Raw git is fine in your own clone.
- The PR base is the open release branch when one is open, else `main`. A stacked PR uses its
  parent branch. Open PRs ready for review, never as drafts.
- Never merge into `main`. A build agent does not merge into the release branch. The PR goes to
  the merge queue (`release-merge-queue`), unless Mahmoud gave release fix authority in this
  session.

Writing and decisions:
- Load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and `communicating-with-mahmoud` before you
  write any report, PR body, comment, artifact, or question. Repeat the reader profile and the
  banned patterns inline in every subagent brief that writes for Mahmoud.
- Put plans, open questions and reports for Mahmoud on an artifact page, with a short chat
  message and the link. Ask one open question at a time.
- Start every GitHub comment with `🤖 _The AI agent says:_ `. Never sign as Claude.
- The agenta repo is public. No customer data, cloud host names, project ids, IPs, secrets, or
  local paths in a PR, commit, issue, or comment.

Loops:
- Cap every fix loop. When a round makes no progress, or after three rounds, stop. Then either
  defer the item (the `defer-todo` skill, with a clean reproduction) or ask Mahmoud. When in doubt
  between fixing now and deferring, defer.
- Keep a run folder `~/agenta-build-<slug>/` with `HANDOFF.md` (current state, next step, open
  questions) and `resources.md` (every clone, lane, container, volume, and sandbox you create).
  Update both at every state change, so another agent can continue cold. Never keep run state in
  `/tmp`.

## Speed

Speed is a goal, and quality must not drop.
- Run independent blocks and agents at the same time. For example, start the QA agents while the
  review loops run, and rerun only the QA cells that the review fixes touch.
- Do not wait for a result the next step does not need. Open the PR as soon as the first slice
  works, so CodeRabbit and CI start early.
- Prefer small fast checks: the targeted test file before the full suite, one API call before a
  browser drive.
- Reuse records. A review-loop record, QA record, or ship record for the current head means that
  gate passed. Do not run it again.
- Do not poll in a loop. Start a background wait and do other work.
- Merge first and fix forward only where the merge queue allows it (never for migrations, auth,
  the runner, or credentials).

## Blocks and the skills that run them

| Block | Skill |
| --- | --- |
| OpenSpec change, viewer page, decision page | `spec-pages` |
| Interface shape review | `design-interfaces` |
| Design simplify review, slop and simplicity loop, correctness and security loop | `review-loop` (with `review-simplify`, `review-slop`, `review-correctness`, `review-security`) |
| Milestones, parallel lanes or clones, cleanup | `milestones` |
| Tests and live QA | `qa-loop` |
| Local deploy for testing | `deploy-worktree-testing`, `debug-local-deployment` |
| Agent runtime checks | `agent-release-gate`, `agent-replay-test` |
| PR body | `write-pr-description` |
| Docs that describe the change | `keep-docs-in-sync`, `write-docs` |
| CI, CodeRabbit, labels, ship record | `pr-ready` |
| Deferred work | `defer-todo` |

319	        if (input.cookie(MOBILE_OPTOUT_COOKIE)) return {kind: "pass"}
320	
321	        // Classic mode ON is the user asking for the desktop app in as many words, through a
322	        // switch that exists to bring them here. It outranks the device heuristic, which is only
323	        // ever a guess about what they want. Without this the two fight and /m wins every time:
324	        // the switch sends them to /w, the device check sends them back, and on a phone there is
325	        // no way out of `/m` at all.

375	        }
376	        return {kind: "pass"}
377	    } catch {

36	  wire field, config schema, tool definition, event payload), load the `design-interfaces`
37	  skill and classify each field by its role before the spec is final.
38	
39	## Step 1: Write the OpenSpec change
40	
41	Read the code first. Every "today" statement needs evidence. Create
42	`openspec/changes/<name>/` with these files:
43	
44	- `proposal.md`: `## Why`, `## What Changes`, `## Capabilities` (New and Modified), and
45	  `## Impact`.
46	- `design.md`: `## Context` (today's behavior, with evidence), `## Goals / Non-Goals`,
47	  `## Decisions` (each decision with a table of options and trade-offs, the chosen option in
48	  bold), then `## Risks / Trade-offs` and `## Migration`.
49	- `specs/<capability>/spec.md`: `## ADDED Requirements` (or `MODIFIED`). Under it,
50	  `### Requirement: <name>` with one sentence that uses SHALL, then one or more
51	  `#### Scenario: <name>` blocks with `- **WHEN** ...` and `- **THEN** ...` lines.
52	- `tasks.md`: numbered sections with `- [ ] 1.1 ...` checkboxes. Mark tasks that can run in
53	  parallel. For a Program, group tasks by milestone; the `milestones` skill splits them.
54	
55	Validate from the repo root:
56	
57	```bash
58	npx @fission-ai/openspec validate <name> --strict
59	```
60	
61	The command runs offline from the npx cache in about one second. With `--strict`, warnings
62	fail the check. The most common warning is a requirement body over 500 characters. Move
63	examples and edge cases into scenarios, or split the requirement.
64	
65	## Step 2: Build the decision page
66	
67	Copy `templates/decision-page.html` from this skill's folder and fill it in:
68	
69	- `<title>`: a name of two to four words.
70	- `h1` and lede: what the feature is, and what the reader decides.
71	- Ability cards (optional): one per part of the feature.
72	- One `<section class="q">` per open question, with:
73	  - a numbered label (`Question 1`);
74	  - a question-style `h2`;
75	  - an example conversation in `.panel`: `.where` names the place, `.msg` rows are the
76	    person, `.msg.bot` rows are the agent's replies;
77	  - 2 to 4 `.opt` rows. Add `.spec` and the "in spec" badge to the option the written spec
78	    uses. Add `.rec` and the "recommended" badge to your recommendation;
79	  - one `.why` line.
80	- Footer: how to answer, by comments or with a line such as "1 recommended, 2 A".
81	
82	Delete the instruction comment at the top before you publish.
83	
84	## Step 3: Render the OpenSpec viewer
85	
86	```bash
87	uv run ~/code/agenta/.claude/skills/spec-pages/scripts/render_openspec.py \
88	  <path/to/openspec/changes/<name>> "<Title, 2 to 4 words>" <out.html> "<source line, for example branch and SHA>"
89	```
90	
91	The script embeds each Markdown file verbatim and renders it in the browser with `marked`
92	(pinned on cdnjs). The page has light and dark themes, sticky tabs, and tables that scroll
93	sideways, and it remembers the last open tab. Tab order: proposal, design, one tab per spec,
94	tasks, then any other Markdown file. It needs `uv` and Python 3.10 or later, and nothing
95	else. The output has a `<title>` but no doctype, `html`, `head` or `body` tags, because the
96	Artifact publisher wraps the page.
97	
98	## Step 4: Publish and take answers
99	
100	Write both pages in a run folder under `~/` (never `/tmp`), then publish each with the
101	Artifact tool. To update a page, write it to the same path and publish again; the URL stays
102	the same. Send Mahmoud a short note with both links and the questions he must answer.
103	
104	When he answers:
105	
106	1. Update the spec files to match each answer, and validate again.
107	2. On the decision page, add `decided` to the section class and change the label to
108	   `Question N, DECIDED: Option X`. Do not delete answered questions.
109	3. Re-render the viewer and publish both pages to the same URLs.
110	
111	## Speed
112	
113	- Read the code for different capabilities with several agents at once, and write the spec
114	  while they report.
115	- Publish the decision page as soon as the open questions are clear. Do not wait for the full
116	  spec before you ask.
117	- Validate and render with the commands above. Each takes seconds, so run them after every
118	  change instead of batching.
119	- Start the design review (`review-loop` in design mode) on the parts of the spec that the

2	name: plain-writing
3	description: >-
4	  Writes and edits prose in a plain and boring style: simple everyday words,
5	  complete sentences, no dashes, no jargon, and no analogies. Use when
6	  drafting or revising documents, Notion pages, reports, summaries, READMEs,
7	  emails, slides, commit messages, or PR descriptions, or when the user asks
8	  to simplify, clean up, tighten, reword, or make writing clearer. Use when
9	  the user invokes /plain-writing deslopify or asks to deslopify an agent
10	  response. Do not apply to code, only to the words around it.
11	license: MIT
12	---
13	
14	# Plain writing
15	
16	The plain writing skill captures how the user wants writing to read: plain,
17	boring, and easy to understand in one pass. Apply it by default when you write
18	for them.
19	
20	There are four groups of rules: word choice and tone, sentences and paragraphs,
21	punctuation and formatting, and patterns to avoid. Each rule has a before and
22	after. After the rules comes the deslopify command.
23	
24	## Word choice and tone
25	
26	1. **Use simple, everyday words.** Don't pick a fancy synonym when a plain word
27	   works. Also avoid words AI tools overuse, e.g., "delve", "tapestry",
28	   "landscape", "robust", "leverage", and "reach".
29	   Before: We leverage the cache to unlock a more robust query experience.
30	   After: We use the cache to make repeated queries faster.
31	
32	2. **No jargon.** Always use human-understandable language, the way two people
33	   talk to each other. Don't invent jargon or shorthand (that is, if a word or
34	   phrase is not in the Merriam Webster dictionary, don't use it). Use
35	   established technical terms only when they are most precise, and briefly
36	   define them when readers may not know them.
37	   Before: The score is a calibrated proxy for whether the property holds.
38	   After: The score estimates how likely the property is to hold.
39	
40	3. **No puffery or empty emphasis.** Drop words that add emphasis but no
41	   information, e.g., "really", "real", "matters", "worth", "carries weight",
42	   "boasts", "a testament to", "pivotal", "renowned", and "quietly". State the
43	   actual point, or cut the sentence.
44	   Before: This result matters, and it carries weight for the design.
45	   After: The scores barely moved, so we can skip the model on most documents.
46	
47	4. **Use consistent terminology and constrain your vocabulary.**
48	   Before: Upload the document. The file is parsed, and the record is saved.
49	   After: Upload the document. The document is parsed and saved.
50	
51	5. **It's ok to use contractions.** They match everyday speech, so use them
52	   freely.
53	   Before: Do not worry, it is not going to overwrite your file.
54	   After: Don't worry, it's not going to overwrite your file.
55	
56	6. **Do not invent hyphenated adjectives.** Avoid a phrase you make up by
57	   joining words with a hyphen to sound compact or clever. If you would not find
58	   it in a dictionary, don't use it. A common compound adjective that people
59	   already use is fine, e.g., "well-crafted".
60	   Before: We added a reveal-style colon to the output.
61	   After: We added a colon that shows the schema.
62	
63	7. **Keep the writing boring, descriptive, and explanatory.** Do not use a
64	   catchy phrase, slogan, clever label, or wording meant to sound memorable.
65	   This rule applies everywhere; to headings, topic sentences, callouts,
66	   labels, summaries, and ordinary prose.
67	   Before: Legal requirements as a floor.
68	   After: Applicable legal constraints.
69	   Before: # The alignment loop
70	   After: # Iterative refinement using development disagreements
71	
72	## Sentences and paragraphs
73	
74	8. **Write complete sentences.** Each sentence should have a subject and a
75	   verb. Do not write fragments, and do not stitch unrelated ideas together with
76	   colons or semicolons. But it is ok to join closely related ideas with plain
77	   conjunctions, like "and", "because", or "so".
78	   Before: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes, and the team meets on
79	   Tuesdays.
80	   After: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes. The team meets on
81	   Tuesdays.
82	
83	9. **When you present a workflow or sequence, walk through it in order.** Use
84	   "First", "Second", "Third", and give each step its own sentence so the
85	   reader can follow it, or break up steps with semicolons.
86	   Before: The groups the features were sorted into were the authors' own
87	   reading, the example posts were written by hand, and finer detail meant
88	   training extra small models and labeling again.
89	   After: First, the authors sorted the features into groups themselves, based on
90	   their own reading of the outputs. Second, they wrote the example posts by
91	   hand. Third, when they wanted finer detail, they trained another small
92	   model, and they labeled the posts again.
93	
94	10. **Organize a paragraph as a topic sentence and then support.** Start each
95	   paragraph or section with a topic sentence that states the main point. Then,
96	   the next sentence should be a supporting example or fact, with an extra
97	   sentence about it if it needs one. Then, introduce more support with a plain
98	   connective like "For example", "Moreover", or "Or".
99	   Before: The parser skips files with no changes. The cache holds the previous
100	   output. Most renders are fast.
101	   After: Most renders are fast. For example, the parser skips files with no
102	   changes, so the server returns early. Moreover, the cache keeps the previous
103	   output, so a repeated render does no work.
104	
105	11. **Never write three or more clauses in one sentence, or three or more
106	    example sentences in a row.** In ordinary prose, a sentence may have one or
107	    two related clauses. Do not pack three or more clauses into one prose
108	    sentence. If you need that many points, use a numbered First / Second / Third
109	    sequence under rule 9, or short bullet points when you are writing a
110	    brief. If list points are examples and you want to inline them, introduce
111	    with "e.g.". Also do not give three or more example sentences back to back
112	    to support the same point.
113	    Before: The parser reads the file, the validator checks the fields, and the
114	    writer saves the record.
115	    After: The parser reads the file, and the validator checks the fields. The
116	    writer then saves the record.
117	
118	12. **Prefer long, explanatory sentences over short, punchy ones.** In ordinary
119	    prose, write the way people explain things out loud: longer sentences with
120	    commas, and the simplest way to say the point. Do not break one thought into
121	    a stack of short sentences, and don't write catchy short phrases. Short
122	    lines are fine only in labeled briefs, bullets, or a First / Second / Third
123	    sequence, e.g., "To do: validate recall on long queries."
124	    Before: The gate runs on every merge. It blocks regressions. Nobody
125	    bypasses it.
126	    After: The gate runs on every merge, and it blocks changes that fail a
127	    regression case. A regression cannot make it to production, unless someone
128	    deliberately overrides the check.
129	    Before: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics. The
130	    change reduced p95 latency from 900 ms to 220 ms. We still need to validate
131	    recall on long queries.
132	    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics, and
133	    p95 latency fell from 900 ms to 220 ms. To do: validate recall on long
134	    queries.
135	
136	13. **Be precise and unambiguous, and cut unnecessary clauses.** Say exactly
137	    what changes, who does what, or by what mechanism. Prefer a concrete
138	    statement over an evocative abstraction, e.g., don't say things like
139	    "improvement stops being guesswork". Also drop trailing or side clauses
140	    that add no fact, e.g., "before we call the work done", "as we move
141	    forward", or "for the time being". Keep the sentence long when the content
142	    needs it, but do not pad it.
143	    Before: With trusted scores, improvement stops being guesswork.
144	    After: With trusted scores, you can measure whether each change helped,
145	    so you keep or revert each change based on the measured result.
146	    Before: We still need to validate recall on long queries before we call
147	    the work done.
148	    After: To do: validate recall on long queries.
149	
150	14. **In chat, give context on the problem.** When you are chatting back and
151	    forth, write for a smart reader who does not have context on the problem,
152	    or who forgot it. Give context on the problem and on what was happening
153	    before. Then say what changed. Keep the setup short. Do not dump the whole
154	    history. Ignore this rule if you are writing an essay.
155	    Before: The exporter now waits on the reset header, and `dotnet test` is
156	    green.
157	    After: The Okta System Log exporter was rereading whole hours, so a retry
158	    could write the same event twice. It now waits using the response reset
159	    header, and the six acceptance tests pass.
160	
161	## Punctuation and formatting
162	
163	15. **No dashes or middle dots.** Do not use em dashes or en dashes, including in
164	    number ranges. Join clauses with a period or "and", and write ranges with
165	    "to". Do not use the middle dot (·) as a separator; use a comma, "and", or
166	    separate lines instead.
167	    Before: The build is fast — it finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
168	    After: The build is fast. It finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
169	
170	16. **Don't use colons to join clauses in ordinary prose.** Do not use a colon
171	    to glue two clauses or to set up a point in essay-like writing. A colon is
172	    fine when you introduce a list. A colon is also fine as a short label in
173	    updates, briefs, status notes, and PR descriptions, e.g., "Summary:",
174	    "Changes:", or "Remaining work:".
175	    Before: Read for the schema: the feature fires.
176	    After: Read for the schema. The feature fires.
177	    Before (allowed in a PR or update): Summary: Replace em dashes in
178	    generated docs.
179	    After (same text is fine): Summary: Replace em dashes in generated docs.
180	
181	17. **Use straight quotes, not curly quotes.**
182	    Before: The system logs each “event” as it happens.
183	    After: The system logs each "event" as it happens.
184	
185	18. **Keep the formatting plain.** Use sentence case in headings. Do not use
186	    bold for decoration.
187	    Before: ## How To Install The Skill
188	    After: ## How to install the skill
189	
190	19. **You can use lists, but do not overuse them.** Keep a list to three or
191	    four points, and nest extra points if you need more. When you are writing
192	    an essay, use lists and tables very sparingly.
193	    Before: Shipped this week:
194	    - dark mode
195	    - an invite link fix
196	    - a schema mismatch that blocked analytics export
197	    - renderer cleanup
198	    - copy edits
199	    - a scored ranking model
200	    - a p95 drop from 900 ms to 220 ms
201	    - untested recall on long queries
202	    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model, and p95 latency fell from
203	    900 ms to 220 ms. The old heuristic path is still in the repo as a
204	    fallback.
205	    - Shipped
206	      - Dark mode
207	      - Invite link fix
208	    - Still open
209	      - Test recall on long queries
210	      - Unblock analytics export
211	
212	## Patterns to avoid
213	
214	20. **Do not give inanimate things fake agency.** Do not write as if a system
215	    or object transforms, decides, or intends on its own when a person or
216	    process is the real actor. Ordinary factual verbs for tools and systems are
217	    fine, e.g., "The API returns JSON", "The job writes the file", or "The
218	    paper argues". Prefer a human or process subject when that is clearer.
219	    Before: The logs become searchable records, once the job finishes.
220	    After: You can search the logs, once the job finishes.
221	
222	21. **No analogies or imagery.** Do not explain by comparing to something else,
223	    and do not use metaphor. Describe the actual thing in literal terms. Write
224	    in a boring way.
225	    Before: The feature index is like a card catalog that the optimizer can flip
226	    through.
227	    After: The feature index is a list of named features. The optimizer can look
228	    up which feature matches a request.
229	
230	22. **Never use negative parallelism of the form "not just X, it is Y" or
231	    "not only X, but Y".** State what the thing is. A plain refusal or
232	    correction is fine, including a short quote of a customer's hype phrase
233	    when you replace it with a concrete fact.
234	    Before: It is not just a parser, it is a full toolchain.
235	    After: It is a parser and a formatter.
236	    Before: We do not describe the API as "enterprise-grade robust," because
237	    that phrase can mean different things.
238	    After: The API has a 99.9% monthly uptime SLO.
239	
240	23. **Do not stack rhetorical questions.** AI writing often asks two or three
241	    rhetorical questions in a row to sound thoughtful. Don't do this. Just state
242	    the problem directly.
243	    Before: Does the tool keep the writer's voice? Does it make the argument
244	    stronger or weaker?
245	    After: We do not yet know whether the tool keeps the writer's voice, or
246	    whether it makes the argument stronger or weaker.
247	
248	24. **Do not use vague demonstrative pronouns.** Do not use "This", "That",
249	    "These", or "Those", especially do not start a sentence with a demonstrative
250	    pronoun, and never begin a paragraph with a sentence that contains a
251	    demonstrative anywhere in it.
252	    Before: That context carries into the next turn.
253	    After: The agent applies the rules you saved on the next turn.
254	
255	25. **Do not open with a count of things.** Never start by announcing how many
256	    points are coming, e.g., "Two cautions." or "Three things to keep in mind."
257	    State the first point directly. If you absolutely must present many things,
258	    use a bullet list instead.
259	    Before: Two cautions. First, the section can drift out of date. Second,
260	    it can balloon if every item gets a sentence.
261	    After: The section can drift out of date, because it duplicates facts
262	    that live elsewhere. It can also balloon if every item gets a sentence.
263	
264	## The deslopify command
265	
266	When the user says `/plain-writing deslopify`, rewrite the previous agent
267	response, or the text after the command, for a sharp CEO or technical reader
268	who has no project context. Return only the rewrite.
269	
270	Start with the main conclusion, then cover the background, how it works, and
271	present all information logically and sequentially. Include technical details
272	the reader needs (standardize on existing well-known terminology, not new
273	terminology), and define unfamiliar terms.

# Communicating with Mahmoud

Doing the work is half the job, and communicating it is the other half. Mahmoud reads the
chat to make decisions, so a correct result written up as a data dump is a failure. He has
said more than once that he would switch models over output he cannot read. Treat every
writeup as part of the deliverable.

For sentence style, load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and follow it. This
skill adds the rules about the reader, the structure, and the process.

## The reader

- Mahmoud is a senior Python developer and architect. He is a beginner in TypeScript and
  frontend work. Explain frontend ideas in terms he can map from the backend.
- He did not read the PR. He does not know the shorthand you built up this session, and he
  does not care in which order you found things.
- For docs, the reader is a stranger with a job, not a teammate. Never assume what they
  know. Phrases such as "the part teams get wrong" or "the first question people ask" are
  banned.

## Structure: context first, then a story

Use this order:

1. Context. What the thing is and why it exists. A reader with no session context must be
   able to follow from here.
2. The choices or parts, one at a time. For each one: how it works, what the user installs
   or does, where things live, and the trade-off.
3. How they combine, with a concrete live example.
4. Limits and gaps.
5. The plan or the options, with a recommendation.

Apply these rules across the whole piece:

- Give each section one axis. Pick the reader's natural questions ("how does it run
  locally?", "what do I install?", "what breaks?") and answer them in order. Do not spread
  one topic across three sections.
- Write headings as plain signposts that state the content. A heading is not a sentence and
  not a clever label.
- Explain how things work today before you describe a change. Show before and after with
  concrete examples: real data shapes and real code.
- If an explanation is short and complicated, rewrite it long and simple.
- Give every decision its reasoning: the problem, the options, the trade-offs, the choice,
  and why. "We do X" with no reason is a review comment waiting to happen.

## Banned patterns

These rules are absolute. Repeat them in every subagent brief.

- No em dashes. Use a period and a new sentence, parentheses, or a semicolon. Check the
  places where they come back: term definitions, trade-off lists, asides, and list item
  separators. The count must be zero.
- No slang: soak, bikeshed, yak-shaving, greenfield, and similar words. Say the plain thing,
  for example "after it has run in real use for a while without problems".
- No drama: "precise and damning", "the one that bit you", "say the word", cute closing
  lines, narrative tension. Debugging and status updates are flat: what happened, what it
  means, what is next.
- No undefined terms. Define every term on first use (runner, vault, sandbox, harness,
  overlay, and any other domain term).
- No bare internal labels. Never use a code such as F-7, C2, Tier 1 or P0 without restating
  it in plain words, every time. He does not remember labels between messages. Prefer names
  that describe themselves, such as "must fix before enabling".
- No meta text in the body. Never write "amended after review", "added per finding", or
  "updated per X" in a doc or report. Provenance goes in PR comments or an appendix.
- Use bold and bullets only when they help quick reading. A wall of bullets should be prose.

## Two lists: what I do, what you do

Always separate "what I will do" from "what you need to do" as two explicit lists. Do not
mix your actions and his actions in one paragraph.

## When he is tired or confused

Drop all compression. Use short sentences with one idea each, numbered steps, and say who
does what at each step. A status update in the middle of the work follows the same rules.

## Questions

- In strategy, brainstorm, and thinking-out-loud conversations, ask one open prose question
  at a time. Do not use multi-select menus. If options help, mention them inline as
  suggestions.
- Use structured multiple choice only for a real, discrete fork in execution work.

## Verify before you assert

- Never write an instruction or claim you have not checked against the code, the config
  file, or the actual behavior. Fluent, confident, wrong instructions cost the reader hours.
  If you cannot verify a claim, cut it.
- Before you hand over docs, run an adversarial pass: a fresh check whose job is to find
  what is still wrong against this skill and `plain-writing`. A self-assessment is not
  evidence.

## Subagent output is your output

- Read everything a subagent wrote (PR body, design doc, report) against this skill before
  you tell Mahmoud it is ready. A rewrite round after he reads it counts as a failure.
- Naming this skill in a brief is not enough. Copy the reader profile and the banned
  patterns above into the brief, word for word.

## PR descriptions

The `write-pr-description` skill, when the repo has it, holds the full procedure. These
rules always apply:

1. Lead with the concrete symptom: what was broken, from the user's point of view.
2. Then the fix in plain words, with a concrete before and after. Show the real data shapes
   when a transformation changed.
3. Then a short section on tests and notes.
4. Add a "How to review" section that walks the diff in reading order.
5. Leave inline comments on the subtle hunks to explain the reason a reviewer would
   otherwise have to work out.

Cut vague bullets that restate the diff, checkbox theater, and "Summary" boilerplate. The
title states the actual change, for example
`fix(api): map OpenInference tool definitions into real tool objects`.
The research agent is still reading the code. I write the onboarding question for Mahmoud when its report arrives, because the question needs the facts about what a new invited user sees today.

content.text:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses the two `max()` paddings given under Responsive, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side, where backgrounds reach that edge while the gutter keeps text and controls clear. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's `env(safe-area-inset-*, 0px)` to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too), a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`, with the band above it painted by a fixed `body::before` (`content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10`) in its background, or in the page's where it starts lower.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#/path`, `#key=value` state or the query string — and the page's own URL changes (`pushState`, path routes, its hash) never show in the viewer's address bar. Only where a page has several views worth bookmarking or sending (tabs, sections, records), name each with a bare token (never `settings`, `sidebar`, `customize`, `upgrade`, `downloads` or anything starting `comment-`, which the viewer keeps), open the one in `location.hash` on load, keep all other state in the page, and give the user each view's link (the artifact's link plus `#token`), because the address bar will not follow them from view to view.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width, written `padding-left: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-left, 0px))` and `padding-right: max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-right, 0px))` so that it also clears a system bar at the phone's side: set it once on `body` or one outer wrapper (where colored bands span the width, on each band's inner wrapper), whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. Put `<meta name="claude:viewport-fit-sides" content="cover">` at the top of the file beside your `<title>`: it promises that the side gutter uses those two `max()` paddings, so the tag goes in only together with both paddings, never alone. An edit of an older page that has neither leaves both out, unless the ask redoes the page's layout. With it the page also runs under a system bar at the phone's side. Anything fixed to a screen edge stays at `0` and adds that edge's inset to its own padding (one that spans the width takes the side gutter too); a floating or absolutely placed control adds the nearby edges' insets to its offsets. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. So that nothing scrolls into view above it, under the host's controls, paint that band with `body::before { content: ""; position: fixed; inset: 0 0 auto; height: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px); z-index: 10; background: ... }`, in the header's own background where the header opens the page and in the page's where the sticky bar starts lower. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside the `:root` padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets the `:root` padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

## Context

All references are to `release/v0.127.3`. The full evidence is in the research note kept with the run.

Today, an invited person takes this path:

1. The email link is `<web_url>/auth?token&email&organization_id&workspace_id&project_id` (`organization_service.py:139-145`). The invite lasts 7 days (`:202`).
2. `isDesktopOnlyLink` holds the link on the old app for every kind of user (`mobileGate/index.ts:343`).
3. The old sign-in sends a new person to `/workspaces/accept?survey=true` and an existing person to `/workspaces/accept` (`web/oss/src/hooks/usePostAuthRedirect.ts:129-157`).
4. The old accept page posts to the accept endpoint through `acceptWorkspaceInvite` (`web/packages/agenta-entities/src/organization/workspaceApi.ts:122-154`). On the cloud edition a new person then sees the `/post-signup` form, which sends `survey sent` (`web/ee/src/components/PostSignupForm/PostSignupForm.tsx:245`).

On `/m` today:

- `useSignInFlow` offers an `onInvite` callback for exactly this purpose (`web/packages/agenta-auth-ui/src/useSignInFlow.ts:157-163`), and `SignInScreen.tsx:49-56` does not pass it.
- `useAuthSuccess` always goes to `/`, and a signed-in visit to `/auth` also goes to `/` (`features/app/authRoute.ts:19-27`).
- `/` is `ContextResolver`, which forwards to a project home. It shows "No projects found." when the person has no project (`ContextResolver.tsx:98-103`).
- A new account gets a pending onboarding mark. Home dismisses the mark when the project has agents, and otherwise starts the full flow (`onboardingPending.ts:70-82`).
- The website `?template=` value already survives sign-in through localStorage with a 30 minute window (`lib/context.ts:29-70`).

Password reset links are `<web_url>/auth/reset-password?token=...&tenantId=public` (`api/oss/src/core/auth/supertokens/config.py:70-73`). They carry `token` and never `organization_id`. `/m` has no reset screen.

## Goals / Non-Goals

Goals:

- A new person and an existing person both join through `/m` from the emailed link, with every sign-in method.
- A signed-in person with a different email sees the old page's mismatch message and can switch account.
- An invite link already in an inbox keeps working.

Non-goals:

- Showing the invite link in `/m` Members settings when email is off (`MembersTab.tsx:90-93`). It is a separate follow-up.
- Removing the old `/workspaces/accept` page. Nothing emails that URL (`organization_service.py` is the only link producer).
- Fixing the API text and check order listed as side bugs in the research note.

## Decisions

### Where the accept screen lives

| Option | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| **`/m/invite`** | Outside `/auth`, so `authRedirectTarget` leaves a signed-in person there. |
| `/m/auth/accept` | `isAuthRoute` would send a signed-in person to `/`, and `authRoute.ts` would need an exception. |
| `/m/workspaces/accept` | Same path as the old page, but workspaces are being removed. |

### How the invite survives sign-in

| Option | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| **localStorage with a 30 minute window, written through `onInvite`** | The same shape as `?template=`. It survives a provider redirect. The token is removed on every final outcome. |
| Carry the values in the OAuth state | It needs changes to the SuperTokens call and does nothing for password sign-in. |
| A cookie | Sent to the server on every request, which a one-time token does not need. |

A person who takes longer than 30 minutes opens the link again, because the link lasts 7 days.

### Who sends the person to the accept screen

| Option | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| **`ContextResolver`, before it resolves a project** | All sign-in paths and the signed-in visit end at `/`, so there is one reader. It also covers a person with no project yet. |
| `useAuthSuccess` plus `OidcCallbackScreen` plus `authRoute` | Three places to keep in step. |

### What the desktop gate tests

| Option | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| **An invite link is an `/auth` link with both `token` and `organization_id`** | Reset links have no `organization_id`, so they keep today's route. |
| Any `/auth?token=` | It would move reset links to `/m`, which has no reset screen. |

The forward runs before the opt-out and Classic mode checks, and it keeps the query. `decideMobileGate` lets `/invite` and an invite link on `/auth` pass, because `desktopRouteFor` would drop the token.

### Onboarding for a new invited person (open on the decision page)

| Option | Trade-off |
| --- | --- |
| **Questions only, then the invited project** | Keeps today's survey event. Needs a small path in onboarding. |
| No questions | The least work. PostHog loses these answers. |
| Leave `/m` as it is | No work. A viewer in an empty project gets steps written for an owner. |

The accept screen turns the pending mark into an invited mark. The onboarding host then shows only the question steps, sends the same events, ends onboarding after the last question, and opens the project home. It also skips seeding tool connections, because that belongs to setting up a new organization.

### Wording

Every string comes from the old page, so nothing is invented. `/m` cannot import `web/oss`, so the strings are copied into `features/invite/`.

## Risks / Trade-offs

- A token sits in localStorage for up to 30 minutes. The old app also stores it there, with no window.
- A shared browser: a second person who signs in within the window reaches the accept screen, and the API answers with the mismatch code. They see the error card, and "Go back to your workspaces" clears the invite.

- A Classic mode person who reloads `/m/` while the invite is pending goes to the old app. The next visit to the link finishes it.

## Migration

No data migration. Deploy order does not matter, because the old app forwards old links and the old app still exists for anything already in progress. Rollback restores the old link path, and any `/m/auth` invite link sent in the meantime still signs in, but it does not accept until the person opens a new invite.
